title: Three fatal pitfalls: Autocorrect, meaningless dates, and rule rot
text: Rewrite you cannot audit. Profile one column, propose the rule, show the evidence, name the owner, and do not change a single value. And this comes back six spellings ranked with counts, the proposed rule underneath it, and the number that matters most, 1,284 rows would newly fail. That is not a bug report. That is a negotiation opening. Is this a data problem or is my rule too strict? This is the part that gets skipped and it is the part that makes the whole thing work. Every proposal stops at a human. 218 ratified, 59 bounced to an owner who actually knows the domain. 41 rejected because the model pattern matched a rule the business does not have. The model proposes, people ratify. Then the rules

Stop being a document. They run on every load. A row that fails a blocking rule never reaches the warehouse. It goes to quarantine carrying the rule that caught it and the person who owns it. The dashboard stops being a score you look at. It becomes a queue somebody works. Three ways this goes wrong. One, let it auto correct and you have inherited a silent edit nobody can trace. Two, every value can be valid and still be meaningless. A column of perfect dates that are all the load date passes everything. Three, rules rot, the business changed, the check did not. Let us recap. The dashboard was never measuring meaning. It was measuring presence and type. Eyes real contribution is not cleaning values. It is

Proposing and maintaining the rules with the evidence attached. Every proposal still stops at a human owner. And the test for all of it, can this rule fail a row and does that failure reach a person? Your turn. Take one table you actually own and paste this. For each column propose one executable expectation with a severity and an owner. Rank them by what a silent failure would cost and list every column where you cannot infer a rule and must ask a human. Watch that last list hardest. The columns it refuses to guess on are the ones your organization never actually decided. The rule, not the report. If this changed how you will look at your next quality dashboard, subscribe.
